Feature: st.scatterplot_matrix_chart — scatterplot matrix (SPLOM) navigation with excentric labeling and lasso query layers

## Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

## Summary

Add `st.scatterplot_matrix_chart`, a native chart command for exploring multivariate/high-dimensional tabular data through a scatterplot matrix (SPLOM). It adds animated "rolling" navigation between attribute pairs, excentric labeling for dense regions, and persistent lasso-based query layers that let you track a subset of rows across different attribute views.

## Why?

Data scientists frequently need to explore relationships across many numeric columns at once. A standard SPLOM grid gives a good overview, but it's hard to inspect any one pair in detail, label individual points in dense clusters, or keep track of the same subset of rows as you move between attribute pairs. This is a longstanding, well-studied interaction pattern in the information-visualization literature, and I think it's a good fit for Streamlit's data-science audience:

- I first built a version of this technique in a data visualization course project over a decade ago (~2012), based on:
  - Pierre Dragicevic ([USER]) et al., "Rolling the Dice: Multidimensional Visual Exploration using Scatterplot Matrix Navigation"
  - Jean-Daniel Fekete ([USER]) and Catherine Plaisant, "Excentric Labeling: Dynamic Neighborhood Labeling for Data Visualization"
  - My original project instructions/write-up from that time (personal notes, kept private)
- A few years ago, a tech company I was working with asked me to use Streamlit, and separately took an interest in this old scatterplot project of mine. Looking back, I read that as an implicit nudge toward combining the two — bringing this navigation technique into Streamlit itself, rather than leaving it as a standalone tool.

Revisiting both experiences, I think this technique deserves a first-class home in Streamlit rather than living on as scattered internal/academic tools.

## How?

I generalized the navigation technique above into a self-contained, WebGL-rendered element and exposed it as a new command, `st.scatterplot_matrix_chart`:

- A small scatterplot cell for every pair of chosen numeric columns, plus one large "detail" plot.
- Left-click a cell to jump to it; right-click (or arrow keys) to "roll" to it through an animated transition across intermediate cells.
- Hover the large plot for an excentric label lens (labels fan out around the cursor in dense regions).
- Up to 8 independent, colored query layers: lasso-select points in the large plot to build a persistent subset, then navigate to other attribute pairs to see how that same subset behaves elsewhere.
- Selections are returned to Python via `on_select="rerun"` as row indices, so they can drive the rest of the app.

A full implementation (backend + frontend + tests) is up for review at #16059.

## Additional Context

- Original ~2012 project instructions (background/inspiration, written by me as a student at the time — personal notes, kept private)
- Academic references: Dragicevic et al., "Rolling the Dice: Multidimensional Visual Exploration using Scatterplot Matrix Navigation"; Fekete & Plaisant, "Excentric Labeling: Dynamic Neighborhood Labeling for Data Visualization"
- Implementation PR: #16059

retrieved_sources.text:
# Create a dynamic navigation menu

`st.navigation` makes it easy to build dynamic navigation menus. You can change the set of pages passed to `st.navigation` with each rerun, which changes the navigation menu to match. This is a convenient feature for creating custom, role-based navigation menus.

This tutorial uses `st.navigation` and `st.Page`, which were introduced in Streamlit version 1.36.0. For an older workaround using the `pages/` directory and `st.page_link`, see [Build a custom navigation menu with `st.page_link`](/develop/tutorials/multipage/st.page_link-nav).

**Notable Changes**

- 📊 [`st.bar_chart`](/develop/api-reference/charts/st.bar_chart) can render charts horizontally.
- ℹ️ [`st.expander`](/develop/api-reference/layout/st.expander) supports adding an icon next to its label.
- 🏗️ [`st.columns`](/develop/api-reference/layout/st.columns) lets you set vertical alignment.
- 📲 Custom components support callback functions ([#8633](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/8633), [#3977](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/3977)).
- 📥 Fragments no longer support rendering widgets outside of their main body ([#8756](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/8756)).
- 🏷️ You can now customize axis labels for [`st.area_chart`](/develop/api-reference/charts/st.area_chart), [`st.bar_chart`](/develop/api-reference/charts/st.bar_chart), [`st.line_chart`](/develop/api-reference/charts/st.line_chart), and [`st.scatter_chart`](/develop/api-reference/charts/st.scatter_chart).
- ⌛ The caching parameter `experimental_allow_widgets` is deprecated ([#8817](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/8817)).
- ❌ Streamlit no longer supports legacy caching. `st.cache` is now an alias for `st.cache_data` and `st.cache_resource` ([#8737](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/8737)).
- ⬆️ Streamlit supports `protobuf` version 5 ([#8627](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/8627)).

**Other Changes**

retrieved_sources.title: Option to set the chart background to something else than the primary background
retrieved_sources.text:
### Problem

As of streamlit 1.16 the chart background color has been changed to match the primary color. This can is some cases make graphs difficult to read. Hence I would like an option to set the chart background separately for all pages in a multipage app. 

I have tried to use
```
import plotly.io as pio
pio.templates.default = "none" 
```
I have also tried to add "plot_bgcolor="grey" to the streamlit theme.

But to no avail, the background color stays the same as the primary color.

I can of cause set theme=None in each st.plotly_chart(), but as my app is large this is cumbersome, and will make it difficult to go back to the streamlit theme. 

My suggestion is therefore twofold.
Make a global option for setting the graph theme, either in the config.toml or on the main page.

Add an option to set the graph background color in config.toml like:
`chartBackgroundColer="#F0F2F6" `
or 
`chartBackgroundColer=secondaryBackgroundColor`

Best regards Kristian

Feature: st.scatterplot_matrix_chart — scatterplot matrix (SPLOM) navigation with excentric labeling and lasso query layers

## Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

## Summary

Add `st.scatterplot_matrix_chart`, a native chart command for exploring multivariate/high-dimensional tabular data through a scatterplot matrix (SPLOM). It adds animated "rolling" navigation between attribute pairs, excentric labeling for dense regions, and persistent lasso-based query layers that let you track a subset of rows across different attribute views.

## Why?

Data scientists frequently need to explore relationships across many numeric columns at once. A standard SPLOM grid gives a good overview, but it's hard to inspect any one pair in detail, label individual points in dense clusters, or keep track of the same subset of rows as you move between attribute pairs. This is a longstanding, well-studied interaction pattern in the information-visualization literature, and I think it's a good fit for Streamlit's data-science audience:

- I first built a version of this technique in a data visualization course project over a decade ago (~2012), based on:
  - Pierre Dragicevic ([USER]) et al., "Rolling the Dice: Multidimensional Visual Exploration using Scatterplot Matrix Navigation"
  - Jean-Daniel Fekete ([USER]) and Catherine Plaisant, "Excentric Labeling: Dynamic Neighborhood Labeling for Data Visualization"
  - My original project instructions/write-up from that time (personal notes, kept private)
- A few years ago, a tech company I was working with asked me to use Streamlit, and separately took an interest in this old scatterplot project of mine. Looking back, I read that as an implicit nudge toward combining the two — bringing this navigation technique into Streamlit itself, rather than leaving it as a standalone tool.

Revisiting both experiences, I think this technique deserves a first-class home in Streamlit rather than living on as scattered internal/academic tools.

## How?

I generalized the navigation technique above into a self-contained, WebGL-rendered element and exposed it as a new command, `st.scatterplot_matrix_chart`:

- A small scatterplot cell for every pair of chosen numeric columns, plus one large "detail" plot.
- Left-click a cell to jump to it; right-click (or arrow keys) to "roll" to it through an animated transition across intermediate cells.
- Hover the large plot for an excentric label lens (labels fan out around the cursor in dense regions).
- Up to 8 independent, colored query layers: lasso-select points in the large plot to build a persistent subset, then navigate to other attribute pairs to see how that same subset behaves elsewhere.
- Selections are returned to Python via `on_select="rerun"` as row indices, so they can drive the rest of the app.

A full implementation (backend + frontend + tests) is up for review at #16059.

## Additional Context

- Original ~2012 project instructions (background/inspiration, written by me as a student at the time — personal notes, kept private)
- Academic references: Dragicevic et al., "Rolling the Dice: Multidimensional Visual Exploration using Scatterplot Matrix Navigation"; Fekete & Plaisant, "Excentric Labeling: Dynamic Neighborhood Labeling for Data Visualization"
- Implementation PR: #16059

Luminosity contrast ratio of link icon is 1.162:1 which is less than required ratio 3:1 in windows. ### Validate input

When specifying a column configuration, you can declare not only the data type of the column but also value restrictions. All column configuration elements allow you to make a column required with the keyword parameter `required=True`.

For Text and Link columns, you can specify the maximum number of characters with `max_chars` or use regular expressions to validate entries through `validate`. Numerical columns, including Number, Date, Time, and Datetime have `min_value` and `max_value` parameters. Selectbox columns have a configurable list of `options`.

The data type for Number columns is `float` by default. Passing a value of type `int` to any of `min_value`, `max_value`, `step`, or `default` will set the type for the column as `int`.

retrieved_sources.text:
### Use `st.rerun`

If your process affects content above your form, another alternative is using an extra rerun. This can be less resource-efficient though, and may be less desirable that the above options.

```python
import streamlit as st

if 'sum' not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state.sum = ''

col1,col2 = st.columns(2)
col1.title('Sum:')
if isinstance(st.session_state.sum, float):
    col2.title(f'{st.session_state.sum:.2f}')

with st.form('addition'):
    a = st.number_input('a')
    b = st.number_input('b')
    submit = st.form_submit_button('add')

# The value of st.session_state.sum is updated at the end of the script rerun,
# so the displayed value at the top in col2 does not show the new sum. Trigger
# a second rerun when the form is submitted to update the value above.
st.session_state.sum = a + b
if submit:
    st.rerun()
```

## Defining pages

`st.Page` lets you define a page. The first and only required argument defines your page source, which can be a Python file or function. When using Python files, your pages may be in a subdirectory (or superdirectory). The path to your page file must always be relative to the entrypoint file. Once you create your page objects, pass them to `st.navigation` to register them as pages in your app.

If you don't define your page title or URL pathname, Streamlit will infer them from the file or function name as described in the multipage apps [Overview](/develop/concepts/multipage-apps/overview#automatic-page-labels-and-urls). However, `st.Page` lets you configure them manually. Within `st.Page`, Streamlit uses `title` to set the page label and title. Additionaly, Streamlit uses `icon` to set the page icon and favicon. If you want to have a different page title and label, or different page icon and favicon, you can use `st.set_page_config` to change the page title and/or favicon. Just call `st.set_page_config` in your entrypoint file or in your page script. You can call `st.set_page_config` multiple times to additively configure your page. Use `st.set_page_config` in your entrypoint file to declare a default configuration, and call it within page scripts to override that default.

The following example uses `st.set_page_config` to set a page title and favicon consistently across pages. Each page will have its own label and icon in the navigation menu, but the browser tab will show a consistent title and favicon on all pages.

retrieved_sources.title: dataframes
retrieved_sources.text:
### Validate input

When specifying a column configuration, you can declare not only the data type of the column but also value restrictions. All column configuration elements allow you to make a column required with the keyword parameter `required=True`.

For Text and Link columns, you can specify the maximum number of characters with `max_chars` or use regular expressions to validate entries through `validate`. Numerical columns, including Number, Date, Time, and Datetime have `min_value` and `max_value` parameters. Selectbox columns have a configurable list of `options`.

The data type for Number columns is `float` by default. Passing a value of type `int` to any of `min_value`, `max_value`, `step`, or `default` will set the type for the column as `int`.

retrieved_sources.title: page-and-navigation
retrieved_sources.text:
## Defining pages

`st.Page` lets you define a page. The first and only required argument defines your page source, which can be a Python file or function. When using Python files, your pages may be in a subdirectory (or superdirectory). The path to your page file must always be relative to the entrypoint file. Once you create your page objects, pass them to `st.navigation` to register them as pages in your app.

If you don't define your page title or URL pathname, Streamlit will infer them from the file or function name as described in the multipage apps [Overview](/develop/concepts/multipage-apps/overview#automatic-page-labels-and-urls). However, `st.Page` lets you configure them manually. Within `st.Page`, Streamlit uses `title` to set the page label and title. Additionaly, Streamlit uses `icon` to set the page icon and favicon. If you want to have a different page title and label, or different page icon and favicon, you can use `st.set_page_config` to change the page title and/or favicon. Just call `st.set_page_config` in your entrypoint file or in your page script. You can call `st.set_page_config` multiple times to additively configure your page. Use `st.set_page_config` in your entrypoint file to declare a default configuration, and call it within page scripts to override that default.

The following example uses `st.set_page_config` to set a page title and favicon consistently across pages. Each page will have its own label and icon in the navigation menu, but the browser tab will show a consistent title and favicon on all pages.

retrieved_sources.title: Altair/Vega-Lite native toolbar: hover the download icon to choose PNG or SVG
retrieved_sources.text:
### How?

Keep the existing native download icon on Altair/Vega-Lite (and other Vega) charts, in the same toolbar row as Fullscreen.

When the pointer hovers that download icon, show a compact dropdown that matches the toolbar (same icon size, radius, colors, light/dark theme). Suggested items:

- Download PNG
- Download SVG

Clicking an item exports from the current Vega view (`toImageURL("png")` / `toImageURL("svg")`) and starts a browser download.

A click with no menu selection can keep today's PNG-only behavior as the default.

I do not need a new `st` command. Optional later: `st.altair_chart(..., download_formats=("png", "svg"))` to choose which items appear. A Python API is nice-to-have; the hover menu on the native icon is the main request.

Please do not bring back the old Vega-Embed ⋯ menu (View Source / Open in Vega Editor). This should stay a Streamlit toolbar control.

packets.initial_report:
Add a `type="pills"` variant to `st.tabs` to show tabs as pills

### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Add a `type` parameter to `st.tabs` with a `"pills"` variant that renders the tab headers as pills (rounded, button-like segments) instead of the default underlined tab bar. Keep the same tab behavior — only the visual style of the tab headers changes.

### Why?

The underlined tab style is great for section navigation, but pill-style tabs are a very common, more compact and prominent look — especially for filters, view switchers, and dashboards. Today users approximate this with `st.pills`/`st.segmented_control` plus manual conditional rendering, which is more boilerplate and doesn't give the clean container-per-tab model that `st.tabs` provides.

### How?

Add a `type` parameter (default preserves today's look):

```python
tab1, tab2, tab3 = st.tabs(["Overview", "Details", "Settings"], type="pills")
with tab1:
    st.write("...")
```

- `type="default"` (or `"underline"`) — current tab bar.
- `type="pills"` — render the tab headers as pills.
- Everything else (content containers, active-tab state, etc.) stays identical.

### Additional Context

- Visually aligns `st.tabs` with the existing pill styling used by `st.pills` / `st.segmented_control`, but with the `st.tabs` container model.
- Design references for the pills style:
  - [Tailwind Plus — Tabs (pill variant)](https://tailwindcss.com/plus/ui-blocks/application-ui/navigation/tabs#component-2a66fc822e8ad55f59321825e5af0980)
  - [Tremor — Tabs, solid variant](https://tremor.so/docs/ui/tabs#example-tabs-solid-variant)
  - [Tremor — Tabs, stretched](https://tremor.so/docs/ui/tabs#example-streched-tabs)

retrieved_sources.text: ## **Version 1.40.0** _Release date: November 6, 2024_ **Highlights** - 💊 Introducing [`st.pills`](/develop/api-reference/widgets/st.pills) to create a single- or multi-select group of pill-buttons. - 🎛️ Introducing [`st.segmented_control`](/develop/api-reference/widgets/st.segmented_control) to create a segmented button or button group. - 🎤 Announcing the general availability of [`st.audio_input`](), a widget to let users record sound with their microphones. **Notable Changes** - ➡️ Markdown renders a limited set of typographical symbols (arrows and comparators). - You can use `:streamlit:` to render the Streamlit logo in [Markdown](/develop/api-reference/text/st.markdown). - 🐍 [`st.text`](/develop/api-reference/text/st.text) wraps text and no longer uses monospace font. - 🪣 You can set `use_container_width` for [`st.image`](/develop/api-reference/media/st.image). `use_column_width` is deprecated. - 📅 [`st.date_input`](/develop/api-reference/widgets/st.date_input) infers the first day of the week from the user’s locale ([#9706](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/9706), [#5215](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/5215)). **Other Changes**

retrieved_sources.section: Add your page and image files
retrieved_sources.text:
### Add your page and image files

1. In `your_repositoy`, create a file named `settings.py`.

1. In `settings.py` add the following stub.

   ```python
   import streamlit as st

   st.header("Settings")
   st.write(f"You are logged in as {st.session_state.role}.")
   ```

   In later steps, you'll create an authentication method that saves the current user's role to `st.session_state.role`. Since you'll be blocking access to this page until a user is logged in, you don't need to initialize the `"role"` key in Session State for this page.

1. Create similar stubs by changing the value of `st.header` for the following six pages:

   ```
   your-repository/
   ├── admin
   │   ├── admin_1.py
   │   └── admin_2.py
   ├── request
   │   ├── request_1.py
   │   └── request_2.py
   └── respond
       ├── respond_1.py
       └── respond_2.py
   ```

   For example, `admin/admin_1.py` should be the following:

   ```python
   import streamlit as st

   st.header("Admin 1")
   st.write(f"You are logged in as {st.session_state.role}.")
   ```

1. Create an `images` subdirectory in `your-repository` and add the following two files:
   - [horizontal_blue.png](/images/horizontal_blue.png)
   - [icon_blue.png](/images/icon_blue.png)

   You now have all the files needed to build your app.

retrieved_sources.text: ## **Version 1.40.0** _Release date: November 6, 2024_ **Highlights** - 💊 Introducing [`st.pills`](/develop/api-reference/widgets/st.pills) to create a single- or multi-select group of pill-buttons. - 🎛️ Introducing [`st.segmented_control`](/develop/api-reference/widgets/st.segmented_control) to create a segmented button or button group. - 🎤 Announcing the general availability of [`st.audio_input`](), a widget to let users record sound with their microphones. **Notable Changes** - ➡️ Markdown renders a limited set of typographical symbols (arrows and comparators). - You can use `:streamlit:` to render the Streamlit logo in [Markdown](/develop/api-reference/text/st.markdown). - 🐍 [`st.text`](/develop/api-reference/text/st.text) wraps text and no longer uses monospace font. - 🪣 You can set `use_container_width` for [`st.image`](/develop/api-reference/media/st.image). `use_column_width` is deprecated. - 📅 [`st.date_input`](/develop/api-reference/widgets/st.date_input) infers the first day of the week from the user’s locale ([#9706](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/9706), [#5215](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/5215)). **Other Changes**

retrieved_sources.text:
### Steps To Reproduce

1. Open the app fresh in Safari (macOS or iOS) — a new tab/window, not a warm reload.
2. Before clicking anything, observe the st.pills widget with selection_mode="multi" and default=None.
3. All options render with the "selected" purple-outline styling, even though nothing has been selected yet.
4. The underlying state is correct (st.write(selected) shows an empty list) — this is a visual-only bug.
5. Does NOT reproduce in Chromium or in Playwright's WebKit engine — only in real Safari.

st.download_button: a filename containing a double quote produces a malformed Content-Disposition header

### Summary

The media endpoint that serves `st.download_button` files builds its `Content-Disposition` header by interpolating the download filename into a quoted string, `filename="{filename}"`, whenever the name is latin-1 encodable. A double quote is latin-1 encodable, so any filename containing one closes the quoted parameter early and the rest of the name spills out as trailing tokens. The emitted header is not valid per RFC 6266, and the name the browser saves the file under is no longer the name the app set.

This needs nothing adversarial to hit. An ordinary filename like `5" x 7" print.jpg` (inch marks) is enough. The name reaches this sink from `st.download_button(file_name=...)`, and since 1.61.0 also from the filename inferred off an uploaded file when `file_name` is omitted.

The safe branch already exists in the same function: a name that is not latin-1 encodable takes `filename*=utf-8''{quote(filename)}`, which percent-encodes and cannot break out. The bug is only which branch a name reaches. Streamlit's own dependency, Starlette, makes the correct choice for the same header in `FileResponse` (`starlette/responses.py`), selecting the quoted form only when `quote(filename) == filename`.

### Reproducible Code Example

Fully in-process against the real media route, no browser needed:

```python
from starlette.applications import Starlette
from starlette.testclient import TestClient
from streamlit.runtime.media_file_storage import MediaFileKind
from streamlit.runtime.memory_media_file_storage import MemoryMediaFileStorage
from streamlit.web.server.starlette.starlette_routes import create_media_routes

# An ordinary filename: a 5 inch by 7 inch print. The inch marks are
# double quotes, which are perfectly valid in a filename.
filename = '5" x 7" print.jpg'

storage = MemoryMediaFileStorage("/media")
file_id = storage.load_and_get_id(
    b"jpeg-bytes", "image/jpeg", MediaFileKind.DOWNLOADABLE, filename
)
client = TestClient(Starlette(routes=create_media_routes(storage, "")))
response = client.get(storage.get_url(file_id))
print(response.headers["content-disposition"])
```

The same header is produced end to end from an app, without touching internals:

```python
import streamlit as st

uploaded = st.file_uploader("upload")
if uploaded:
    # The inch marks in the file_name break the emitted header.
    st.download_button("download", data=uploaded, file_name='5" x 7" print.jpg')
```

### Steps To Reproduce

1. `pip install streamlit==1.61.1`
2. Save the first snippet above as `repro.py`.
3. Run `python repro.py`.
4. Observe the printed header: `attachment; filename="5" x 7" print.jpg"`. The `filename` parameter is terminated by the first `"` after `5`, so the value a conforming parser reads is not the name the app set.

### Expected Behavior

A filename with characters that are not safe unescaped inside a quoted string (a double quote, a semicolon, a space) should still be carried faithfully in a valid header, using the RFC 5987 `filename*=` form, exactly as the non-latin-1 branch already does and as Starlette's `FileResponse` does:

```
attachment; filename*=utf-8''5%22%20x%207%22%20print.jpg
```

### Current Behavior

The name is interpolated into `filename="..."` verbatim, so the double quote closes the parameter:

```
attachment; filename="5" x 7" print.jpg"
```

That is not a valid RFC 6266 header: the quoted string ends at the first unescaped `"`, and everything after it is stray tokens. A name that also contains `;` can introduce additional `Content-Disposition` parameters, so the header's structure ends up controlled by the filename rather than by Streamlit.

Root cause, `lib/streamlit/web/server/starlette/starlette_routes.py` in `_media_endpoint`:

```python
try:
    filename.encode("latin1")
    disposition = f'filename="{filename}"'
except UnicodeEncodeError:
    disposition = f"filename*=utf-8''{quote(filename)}"
headers["Content-Disposition"] = f"attachment; {disposition}"
```

The branch is selected on latin-1 encodability, but the property that matters is whether the value is safe unescaped inside a quoted parameter, and `"`, `;` and space are all latin-1 encodable.

### Fix direction

Select the branch the way Starlette's `FileResponse` does in `starlette/responses.py`: emit the plain `filename="..."` form only when `quote(filename) == filename`, and fall back to `filename*=utf-8''{quote(filename)}` otherwise. This is a strict superset of the current safe branch (every non-latin-1 name still percent-encodes) and additionally routes latin-1 names that need escaping onto the safe form. Plain ASCII names like `report.pdf` keep the quoted form unchanged.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.61.1 (present since 1.60.0; also on current `develop`)
- Python version: 3.10 - 3.14
- Operating System: any
- Browser: n/a (backend header construction; the visible effect is the saved download name)

summary.problem:
st.download_button: a filename containing a double quote produces a malformed Content-Disposition header

### Summary

The media endpoint that serves `st.download_button` files builds its `Content-Disposition` header by interpolating the download filename into a quoted string, `filename="{filename}"`, whenever the name is latin-1 encodable. A double quote is latin-1 encodable, so any filename containing one closes the quoted parameter early and the rest of the name spills out as trailing tokens. The emitted header is not valid per RFC 6266, and the name the browser saves the file under is no longer the name the app set.

This needs nothing adversarial to hit. An ordinary filename like `5" x 7" print.jpg` (inch marks) is enough. The name reaches this sink from `st.download_button(file_name=...)`, and since 1.61.0 also from the filename inferred off an uploaded file when `file_name` is omitted.

The safe branch already exists in the same function: a name that is not latin-1 encodable takes `filename*=utf-8''{quote(filename)}`, which percent-encodes and cannot break out. The bug is only which branch a name reaches. Streamlit's own dependency, Starlette, makes the correct choice for the same header in `FileResponse` (`starlette/responses.py`), selecting the quoted form only when `quote(filename) == filename`.

### Reproducible Code Example

Fully in-process against the real media route, no browser needed:

```python
from starlette.applications import Starlette
from starlette.testclient import TestClient
from streamlit.runtime.media_file_storage import MediaFileKind
from streamlit.runtime.memory_media_file_storage import MemoryMediaFileStorage
from streamlit.web.server.starlette.starlette_routes import create_media_routes

# An ordinary filename: a 5 inch by 7 inch print. The inch marks are
# double quotes, which are perfectly valid in a filename.
filename = '5" x 7" print.jpg'

storage = MemoryMediaFileStorage("/media")
file_id = storage.load_and_get_id(
    b"jpeg-bytes", "image/jpeg", MediaFileKind.DOWNLOADABLE, filename
)
client = TestClient(Starlette(routes=create_media_routes(storage, "")))
response = client.get(storage.get_url(file_id))
print(response.headers["content-disposition"])
```

The same header is produced end to end from an app, without touching internals:

```python
import streamlit as st

uploaded = st.file_uploader("upload")
if uploaded:

retrieved_sources.title: where-file-uploader-store-when-deleted
retrieved_sources.section: Where does st.file_uploader store uploaded files and when do they get deleted?
retrieved_sources.text:
# Where does st.file_uploader store uploaded files and when do they get deleted?

When you upload a file using [`st.file_uploader`](/develop/api-reference/widgets/st.file_uploader), the data are copied to the Streamlit backend via the browser, and contained in a BytesIO buffer in Python memory (i.e. RAM, not disk). The data will persist in RAM until the Streamlit app re-runs from top-to-bottom, which is on each widget interaction. If you need to save the data that was uploaded between runs, then you can [cache](/develop/concepts/architecture/caching) it so that Streamlit persists it across re-runs.

As files are stored in memory, they get deleted immediately as soon as they’re not needed anymore.

This means Streamlit removes a file from memory when:

- The user uploads another file, replacing the original one
- The user clears the file uploader
- The user closes the browser tab where they uploaded the file

Related forum posts:

- https://discuss.streamlit.io/t/streamlit-sharing-fileupload-where-does-it-go/9267
- https://discuss.streamlit.io/t/how-to-update-the-uploaded-file-using-file-uploader/13512/

retrieved_sources.title: architecture
retrieved_sources.text:
## WebSockets and session management

While most Streamlit app developers don’t need to interact directly with WebSockets, understanding their role is important for advanced deployments, custom components, or managing connections at scale.

Streamlit’s server is built on the Tornado web framework, which uses WebSockets to maintain a persistent, two-way communication channel between the client and server. This persistent connection allows the server to push real-time updates to the client and maintain session context for each user. Each browser tab or window creates its own WebSocket connection, resulting in a separate session within your app.

In large-scale or production deployments, load balancing and server replication are common. However, the way Streamlit handles sessions and local (server) files requires special consideration in these environments. When a client requests media (such as an image or audio file) via HTTP, there is no session context attached to that request. In deployments with multiple server replicas or load balancers, the HTTP request for the media file might be routed to a different server than the one handling the user’s WebSocket connection and session information. If the media file isn’t available on all replicas, you may encounter errors like `MediaFileStorageError: Bad filename`. Any command that allows the user to upload files can also be impacted and may raise HTTP status code 400.

retrieved_sources.title: static-file-serving
retrieved_sources.text:
# Static file serving

Streamlit apps can host and serve small, static media files to support media embedding use cases that
won't work with the normal [media elements](/develop/api-reference/media).

To enable this feature, set `enableStaticServing = true` under `[server]` in your config file,
or environment variable `STREAMLIT_SERVER_ENABLE_STATIC_SERVING=true`.

Media stored in the folder `./static/` relative to the running app file is served at path
`app/static/[filename]`, such as `http://localhost:8501/app/static/cat.png`.

retrieved_sources.title: download_button with data=callable runs without ScriptRunContext
retrieved_sources.text:
### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.52.2
- Python version: 3.13
- Operating System: Win
- Browser: Chrome

Somehow I missed this issue https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/13337
Closing as duplicate

Confirming this from a production incident — and it's a bit worse than "missing ScriptRunContext produces a warning": inside that thread, `st.session_state` reads return stale values and `@st.cache_data`-wrapped calls silently return whatever was already cached, **with no error and no warning**. Both just look like they worked.

Our incident: a `data=callable` on `st.download_button` called into functions that (transitively) read `@st.cache_data`-cached helpers. Because those calls run outside `ScriptRunContext`, they picked up cached results from a *different* request context — users occasionally downloaded a file that didn't match what they'd just generated on screen, with nothing in the logs to explain why. We only found the mechanism by tracing the full call graph of the callable, not just inspecting it — a lambda that looks pure can still be unsafe if anything it calls touches cached/session state indirectly.

We ended up moving off lazy `data=` entirely (eager bytes, pre-warmed at save time) because we couldn't make the callable's dependency tree provably free of session/cache reads. For anyone hitting this: if your callable calls anything that isn't a pure function of its arguments, the missing context isn't just a perf/warning issue, it's a correctness one.

packets.initial_report:
st.download_button: a filename containing a double quote produces a malformed Content-Disposition header

### Summary

The media endpoint that serves `st.download_button` files builds its `Content-Disposition` header by interpolating the download filename into a quoted string, `filename="{filename}"`, whenever the name is latin-1 encodable. A double quote is latin-1 encodable, so any filename containing one closes the quoted parameter early and the rest of the name spills out as trailing tokens. The emitted header is not valid per RFC 6266, and the name the browser saves the file under is no longer the name the app set.

This needs nothing adversarial to hit. An ordinary filename like `5" x 7" print.jpg` (inch marks) is enough. The name reaches this sink from `st.download_button(file_name=...)`, and since 1.61.0 also from the filename inferred off an uploaded file when `file_name` is omitted.

The safe branch already exists in the same function: a name that is not latin-1 encodable takes `filename*=utf-8''{quote(filename)}`, which percent-encodes and cannot break out. The bug is only which branch a name reaches. Streamlit's own dependency, Starlette, makes the correct choice for the same header in `FileResponse` (`starlette/responses.py`), selecting the quoted form only when `quote(filename) == filename`.

### Reproducible Code Example

Fully in-process against the real media route, no browser needed:

```python
from starlette.applications import Starlette
from starlette.testclient import TestClient
from streamlit.runtime.media_file_storage import MediaFileKind
from streamlit.runtime.memory_media_file_storage import MemoryMediaFileStorage
from streamlit.web.server.starlette.starlette_routes import create_media_routes

# An ordinary filename: a 5 inch by 7 inch print. The inch marks are
# double quotes, which are perfectly valid in a filename.
filename = '5" x 7" print.jpg'

storage = MemoryMediaFileStorage("/media")
file_id = storage.load_and_get_id(
    b"jpeg-bytes", "image/jpeg", MediaFileKind.DOWNLOADABLE, filename
)
client = TestClient(Starlette(routes=create_media_routes(storage, "")))
response = client.get(storage.get_url(file_id))
print(response.headers["content-disposition"])
```

The same header is produced end to end from an app, without touching internals:

```python
import streamlit as st

uploaded = st.file_uploader("upload")
if uploaded:
    # The inch marks in the file_name break the emitted header.
    st.download_button("download", data=uploaded, file_name='5" x 7" print.jpg')
```

### Steps To Reproduce

1. `pip install streamlit==1.61.1`
2. Save the first snippet above as `repro.py`.
3. Run `python repro.py`.
4. Observe the printed header: `attachment; filename="5" x 7" print.jpg"`. The `filename` parameter is terminated by the first `"` after `5`, so the value a conforming parser reads is not the name the app set.

### Expected Behavior

A filename with characters that are not safe unescaped inside a quoted string (a double quote, a semicolon, a space) should still be carried faithfully in a valid header, using the RFC 5987 `filename*=` form, exactly as the non-latin-1 branch already does and as Starlette's `FileResponse` does:

```
attachment; filename*=utf-8''5%22%20x%207%22%20print.jpg
```

### Current Behavior

The name is interpolated into `filename="..."` verbatim, so the double quote closes the parameter:

```
attachment; filename="5" x 7" print.jpg"
```

That is not a valid RFC 6266 header: the quoted string ends at the first unescaped `"`, and everything after it is stray tokens. A name that also contains `;` can introduce additional `Content-Disposition` parameters, so the header's structure ends up controlled by the filename rather than by Streamlit.

Root cause, `lib/streamlit/web/server/starlette/starlette_routes.py` in `_media_endpoint`:

```python
try:
    filename.encode("latin1")
    disposition = f'filename="{filename}"'
except UnicodeEncodeError:
    disposition = f"filename*=utf-8''{quote(filename)}"
headers["Content-Disposition"] = f"attachment; {disposition}"
```

The branch is selected on latin-1 encodability, but the property that matters is whether the value is safe unescaped inside a quoted parameter, and `"`, `;` and space are all latin-1 encodable.

### Fix direction

Select the branch the way Starlette's `FileResponse` does in `starlette/responses.py`: emit the plain `filename="..."` form only when `quote(filename) == filename`, and fall back to `filename*=utf-8''{quote(filename)}` otherwise. This is a strict superset of the current safe branch (every non-latin-1 name still percent-encodes) and additionally routes latin-1 names that need escaping onto the safe form. Plain ASCII names like `report.pdf` keep the quoted form unchanged.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.61.1 (present since 1.60.0; also on current `develop`)
- Python version: 3.10 - 3.14
- Operating System: any
- Browser: n/a (backend header construction; the visible effect is the saved download name)

summary.problem:
st.download_button: a filename containing a double quote produces a malformed Content-Disposition header

### Summary

The media endpoint that serves `st.download_button` files builds its `Content-Disposition` header by interpolating the download filename into a quoted string, `filename="{filename}"`, whenever the name is latin-1 encodable. A double quote is latin-1 encodable, so any filename containing one closes the quoted parameter early and the rest of the name spills out as trailing tokens. The emitted header is not valid per RFC 6266, and the name the browser saves the file under is no longer the name the app set.

This needs nothing adversarial to hit. An ordinary filename like `5" x 7" print.jpg` (inch marks) is enough. The name reaches this sink from `st.download_button(file_name=...)`, and since 1.61.0 also from the filename inferred off an uploaded file when `file_name` is omitted.

The safe branch already exists in the same function: a name that is not latin-1 encodable takes `filename*=utf-8''{quote(filename)}`, which percent-encodes and cannot break out. The bug is only which branch a name reaches. Streamlit's own dependency, Starlette, makes the correct choice for the same header in `FileResponse` (`starlette/responses.py`), selecting the quoted form only when `quote(filename) == filename`.

### Reproducible Code Example

Fully in-process against the real media route, no browser needed:

```python
from starlette.applications import Starlette
from starlette.testclient import TestClient
from streamlit.runtime.media_file_storage import MediaFileKind
from streamlit.runtime.memory_media_file_storage import MemoryMediaFileStorage
from streamlit.web.server.starlette.starlette_routes import create_media_routes

# An ordinary filename: a 5 inch by 7 inch print. The inch marks are
# double quotes, which are perfectly valid in a filename.
filename = '5" x 7" print.jpg'

storage = MemoryMediaFileStorage("/media")
file_id = storage.load_and_get_id(
    b"jpeg-bytes", "image/jpeg", MediaFileKind.DOWNLOADABLE, filename
)
client = TestClient(Starlette(routes=create_media_routes(storage, "")))
response = client.get(storage.get_url(file_id))
print(response.headers["content-disposition"])
```

retrieved_sources.title: architecture
retrieved_sources.text:
### Session affinity or stickiness

In general, you can do one of the following to resolve or reduce this limitation:

- Enable session affinity (also known as stickiness) in your proxy. This ensures that all requests from a user’s session are handled by the same server instance.
- Convert media to a Base64 encoded data URI before passing it to a Streamlit command. This passes the media data through the WebSocket instead of using Streamlit's media storage which is accessed through HTTP requests.
- Save dynamically generated files to a stable location outside of your server replicas (e.g. S3 storage), and pass the external URLs to Streamlit commands. This avoids Streamlit's media storage.

Enabling session affinity is a general solution which resolves the limitation for both media files and uploaded files. For configuration details, consult your deployment platform’s documentation.

Using Base64 encoded data URIs or external file storage can straightforwardly resolve the limitation for media files, but are not complete solutions to resolve the limitation for file uploads. For more information, see GitHub issue [#4173](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/4173).

retrieved_sources.section: Where does st.file_uploader store uploaded files and when do they get deleted?
retrieved_sources.text:
# Where does st.file_uploader store uploaded files and when do they get deleted?

When you upload a file using [`st.file_uploader`](/develop/api-reference/widgets/st.file_uploader), the data are copied to the Streamlit backend via the browser, and contained in a BytesIO buffer in Python memory (i.e. RAM, not disk). The data will persist in RAM until the Streamlit app re-runs from top-to-bottom, which is on each widget interaction. If you need to save the data that was uploaded between runs, then you can [cache](/develop/concepts/architecture/caching) it so that Streamlit persists it across re-runs.

As files are stored in memory, they get deleted immediately as soon as they’re not needed anymore.

This means Streamlit removes a file from memory when:

- The user uploads another file, replacing the original one
- The user clears the file uploader
- The user closes the browser tab where they uploaded the file

Related forum posts:

- https://discuss.streamlit.io/t/streamlit-sharing-fileupload-where-does-it-go/9267
- https://discuss.streamlit.io/t/how-to-update-the-uploaded-file-using-file-uploader/13512/

retrieved_sources.text:
The ``UploadedFile`` class is a subclass of ``BytesIO``, and
    therefore is "file-like". This means you can pass an instance of it
    anywhere a file is expected.

Examples
--------
**Example 1: Accept a single file at a time**

>>> import streamlit as st
>>> import pandas as pd
>>> from io import StringIO
>>>
>>> uploaded_file = st.file_uploader("Choose a file")
>>> if uploaded_file is not None:
...     # To read file as bytes:
...     bytes_data = uploaded_file.getvalue()
...     st.write(bytes_data)
>>>
...     # To convert to a string based IO:
...     stringio = StringIO(uploaded_file.getvalue().decode("utf-8"))
...     st.write(stringio)
>>>
...     # To read file as string:
...     string_data = stringio.read()
...     st.write(string_data)
>>>
...     # Can be used wherever a "file-like" object is accepted:
...     dataframe = pd.read_csv(uploaded_file)
...     st.write(dataframe)

**Example 2: Accept multiple files at a time**

>>> import pandas as pd
>>> import streamlit as st
>>>
>>> uploaded_files = st.file_uploader(
...     "Upload data", accept_multiple_files=True, type="csv"
... )
>>> for uploaded_file in uploaded_files:
...     df = pd.read_csv(uploaded_file)
...     st.write(df)

.. output::
   https://doc-file-uploader.streamlit.app/
   height: 375px

**Example 3: Accept an entire directory**

>>> import streamlit as st
>>>
>>> uploaded_files = st.file_uploader(
...     "Upload images", accept_multiple_files="directory", type=["jpg", "png"]
... )
>>> for uploaded_file in uploaded_files:
...     st.image(uploaded_file)

retrieved_sources.text:
See also https://discuss.streamlit.io/t/awesome-streamlit-org-change-log/1414/7?u=marc

```
# pylint: disable=line-too-long
"""This is example shows how to **upload multiple files** via the
[File Uploader Widget](https://streamlit.io/docs/api.html?highlight=file%20upload#streamlit.file_uploader)

As far as I can see you can only upload one file at a time. So if you need multiple files in your
app, you need to store them in a static List or Dictionary. Alternatively they should be uploaded
as one .zip file.

Please note that file uploader is a **bit problematic** because
- You can only upload one file at the time.
- You get no additional information on the file like name, size, upload time, type etc. So you
cannot distinguish the files without reading the content.
- every time you interact with any widget, the script is rerun and you risk processing or storing
the file again!
- The file uploader widget is not cleared when you clear the cache and there is no way to clear the
file uploader widget programmatically.

This example was based on
[Discourse 1445](https://discuss.streamlit.io/t/uploading-multiple-files-with-file-uploader/1445)
"""
# pylint: enable=line-too-long
from typing import Dict

import streamlit as st


@st.cache(allow_output_mutation=True)
def get_static_store() -> Dict:
    """This dictionary is initialized once and can be used to store the files uploaded"""
    return {}


def main():
    """Run this function to run the app"""
    static_store = get_static_store()

    st.info(__doc__)
    result = st.file_uploader("Upload", type="py")
    if result:
        # Process you file here
        value = result.getvalue()

        # And add it to the static_store if not already in
        if not value in static_store.values():
            static_store[result] = value
    else:
        static_store.clear()  # Hack to clear list if the user clears the cache and reloads the page
        st.info("Upload one or more `.py` files.")

    if st.button("Clear file list"):
        static_store.clear()
    if st.checkbox("Show file list?", True):
        st.write(list(static_store.keys()))
    if st.checkbox("Show content of files?"):
        for value in static_store.values():
            st.code(value)


main()
```

Frontend uses user-controlled file name as FormData field name in file upload

### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar issues.
- [x] I added a very descriptive title to this issue.
- [x] I have provided sufficient information below to help reproduce this issue.

### Summary

In `uploadFileUploaderFile`, the frontend constructs a `FormData` object for file uploads using the file's own name (`name`) as the multipart form-data field name: `form.append(name, file, fileName)`. Because the backend does not rely on this dynamic field name and files are uploaded individually, using the user-controlled filename introduces potential security risks, such as bypassing security filters, WAFs, or length restrictions designed for form field names.

retrieved_sources.title: where-file-uploader-store-when-deleted
retrieved_sources.section: Where does st.file_uploader store uploaded files and when do they get deleted?
retrieved_sources.text:
# Where does st.file_uploader store uploaded files and when do they get deleted?

When you upload a file using [`st.file_uploader`](/develop/api-reference/widgets/st.file_uploader), the data are copied to the Streamlit backend via the browser, and contained in a BytesIO buffer in Python memory (i.e. RAM, not disk). The data will persist in RAM until the Streamlit app re-runs from top-to-bottom, which is on each widget interaction. If you need to save the data that was uploaded between runs, then you can [cache](/develop/concepts/architecture/caching) it so that Streamlit persists it across re-runs.

As files are stored in memory, they get deleted immediately as soon as they’re not needed anymore.

This means Streamlit removes a file from memory when:

- The user uploads another file, replacing the original one
- The user clears the file uploader
- The user closes the browser tab where they uploaded the file

Related forum posts:

- https://discuss.streamlit.io/t/streamlit-sharing-fileupload-where-does-it-go/9267
- https://discuss.streamlit.io/t/how-to-update-the-uploaded-file-using-file-uploader/13512/

retrieved_sources.title: architecture
retrieved_sources.text:
## WebSockets and session management

While most Streamlit app developers don’t need to interact directly with WebSockets, understanding their role is important for advanced deployments, custom components, or managing connections at scale.

Streamlit’s server is built on the Tornado web framework, which uses WebSockets to maintain a persistent, two-way communication channel between the client and server. This persistent connection allows the server to push real-time updates to the client and maintain session context for each user. Each browser tab or window creates its own WebSocket connection, resulting in a separate session within your app.

In large-scale or production deployments, load balancing and server replication are common. However, the way Streamlit handles sessions and local (server) files requires special consideration in these environments. When a client requests media (such as an image or audio file) via HTTP, there is no session context attached to that request. In deployments with multiple server replicas or load balancers, the HTTP request for the media file might be routed to a different server than the one handling the user’s WebSocket connection and session information. If the media file isn’t available on all replicas, you may encounter errors like `MediaFileStorageError: Bad filename`. Any command that allows the user to upload files can also be impacted and may raise HTTP status code 400.

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Deploy the Streamlit app to Streamlit Community Cloud

מסמך.pdf (Hebrew)

اختبار.pdf (Arabic)

测试.pdf (Chinese)

テスト.pdf (Japanese)

file_🙂.pdf (Emoji)

"AxiosError: Request failed with status code 400"

In `uploadFileUploaderFile`, the frontend constructs a `FormData` object for file uploads using the file's own name (`name`) as the multipart form-data field name: `form.append(name, file, fileName)`. Because the backend does not rely on this dynamic field name and files are uploaded individually, using the user-controlled filename introduces potential security risks, such as bypassing security filters, WAFs, or length restrictions designed for form field names.


```typescript
const form = new FormData()
const { name, webkitRelativePath } = file
// For directory uploads, use the relative path as fileName to preserve directory structure
const fileName = webkitRelativePath || name
form.append(name, file, fileName)

```

### Proposed Solution

Replace the dynamic `name` variable with a static string (such as `"file"`), since files are handled individually and the backend does not require the field name to match the filename.

```typescript
const form = new FormData()
const { name, webkitRelativePath } = file
// For directory uploads, use the relative path as fileName to preserve directory structure
const fileName = webkitRelativePath || name
form.append("file", file, fileName)

```


### Security Impact

* **User-Controlled Field Names:** Attackers can manipulate file names (including special characters, injection sequences, or excessive lengths) which are then directly injected into the multipart form-data structure as the field name.
* **Validation & WAF Bypasses:** Backend proxies, Web Application Firewalls (WAFs), or API gateways often enforce strict validation rules (character sets, maximum length) on form field names. Allowing client-side filenames to define these keys can lead to unexpected parsing behavior or security filter evasion.

### Reproducible Code Example

```Python
import streamlit as st

uploaded_file = st.file_uploader("Choose a file")
if uploaded_file is not None:
    st.write(f"Uploaded filename: {uploaded_file.name}")
```

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Run the provided Python script using Streamlit.
2. Open your browser's Developer Tools and navigate to the **Network** tab.
3. Upload a file via the file uploader (e.g., a file named `malicious_name_test.txt`).
4. Inspect the multipart `form-data` payload sent in the upload request.
5. Observe that the form field `name` attribute equals the file's name (`malicious_name_test.txt`) instead of a static, controlled identifier.

### Expected Behavior

The multipart form-data request should use a static, predefined field name (such as `name="file"`) for the upload payload, ensuring that the form field name is fully controlled and sanitized, while the actual file name/path remains properly preserved only in the filename parameter.

### Current Behavior

When a file is uploaded through `st.file_uploader`, the frontend dynamically sets the multipart form-data field name to match the uploaded file's name (`form.append(name, file, fileName)`). As a result, user-controlled strings, special characters, and arbitrary lengths are directly injected into the request's form field name.

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.58.0
- Python version: 3.11
- Operating System: Windows
- Browser: Chrome

_No response_

retrieved_sources.text:
# Where does st.file_uploader store uploaded files and when do they get deleted?

When you upload a file using [`st.file_uploader`](/develop/api-reference/widgets/st.file_uploader), the data are copied to the Streamlit backend via the browser, and contained in a BytesIO buffer in Python memory (i.e. RAM, not disk). The data will persist in RAM until the Streamlit app re-runs from top-to-bottom, which is on each widget interaction. If you need to save the data that was uploaded between runs, then you can [cache](/develop/concepts/architecture/caching) it so that Streamlit persists it across re-runs.

As files are stored in memory, they get deleted immediately as soon as they’re not needed anymore.

This means Streamlit removes a file from memory when:

- The user uploads another file, replacing the original one
- The user clears the file uploader
- The user closes the browser tab where they uploaded the file

Related forum posts:

retrieved_sources.title: file_uploader API docstrings 1.49.0
retrieved_sources.text:
The ``UploadedFile`` class is a subclass of ``BytesIO``, and
    therefore is "file-like". This means you can pass an instance of it
    anywhere a file is expected.

Examples
--------
**Example 1: Accept a single file at a time**

>>> import streamlit as st
>>> import pandas as pd
>>> from io import StringIO
>>>
>>> uploaded_file = st.file_uploader("Choose a file")
>>> if uploaded_file is not None:
...     # To read file as bytes:
...     bytes_data = uploaded_file.getvalue()
...     st.write(bytes_data)
>>>
...     # To convert to a string based IO:
...     stringio = StringIO(uploaded_file.getvalue().decode("utf-8"))
...     st.write(stringio)
>>>
...     # To read file as string:
...     string_data = stringio.read()
...     st.write(string_data)
>>>
...     # Can be used wherever a "file-like" object is accepted:
...     dataframe = pd.read_csv(uploaded_file)
...     st.write(dataframe)

**Example 2: Accept multiple files at a time**

>>> import pandas as pd
>>> import streamlit as st
>>>
>>> uploaded_files = st.file_uploader(
...     "Upload data", accept_multiple_files=True, type="csv"
... )
>>> for uploaded_file in uploaded_files:
...     df = pd.read_csv(uploaded_file)
...     st.write(df)

.. output::
   https://doc-file-uploader.streamlit.app/
   height: 375px

**Example 3: Accept an entire directory**

>>> import streamlit as st
>>>
>>> uploaded_files = st.file_uploader(
...     "Upload images", accept_multiple_files="directory", type=["jpg", "png"]
... )
>>> for uploaded_file in uploaded_files:
...     st.image(uploaded_file)

retrieved_sources.title: architecture
retrieved_sources.text:
## WebSockets and session management

While most Streamlit app developers don’t need to interact directly with WebSockets, understanding their role is important for advanced deployments, custom components, or managing connections at scale.

Streamlit’s server is built on the Tornado web framework, which uses WebSockets to maintain a persistent, two-way communication channel between the client and server. This persistent connection allows the server to push real-time updates to the client and maintain session context for each user. Each browser tab or window creates its own WebSocket connection, resulting in a separate session within your app.

In large-scale or production deployments, load balancing and server replication are common. However, the way Streamlit handles sessions and local (server) files requires special consideration in these environments. When a client requests media (such as an image or audio file) via HTTP, there is no session context attached to that request. In deployments with multiple server replicas or load balancers, the HTTP request for the media file might be routed to a different server than the one handling the user’s WebSocket connection and session information. If the media file isn’t available on all replicas, you may encounter errors like `MediaFileStorageError: Bad filename`. Any command that allows the user to upload files can also be impacted and may raise HTTP status code 400.

Clarify st.number_input return type when value= int | None

### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar issues.
- [x] I added a very descriptive title to this issue.
- [x] I have provided sufficient information below to help reproduce this issue.

### Summary

Passing a typed variable of int | None to the value parameter for number_input returns a float | None type.

I expected this to be int | None, and that this is how you are expected to create an empty input field, that accepts integers only, assuming the step parameter would default to 1, but it appears that strictly requires value to be int.

If you set step=1, then static type checking works as expected, resolving to int | None.

### Reproducible Code Example

```Python
import streamlit as st

default_value: int | None = None

number = st.number_input(
    "Input number",
    value=default_value,
)

if number:
    assert isinstance(number, int)
    print('Number is an int')
```

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Run example
2. Input number

### Expected Behavior

Prints 'Number is an int'

### Current Behavior

Assertion fails.

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.59.1
- Python version: 3.12
- Operating System: Windows
- Browser: Edge


### Additional Information

_No response_

retrieved_sources.title: get-started
retrieved_sources.text:
### How to inspect elements

All elements, including widgets, have a universal `.value` property. This returns the contents of the element. For widgets, this is the same as the return value or value in Session State. For non-input elements, this will be the value of the primary contents argument. For example, `.value` returns the value of `body` for `st.markdown` or `st.error`. It returns the value of `data` for `st.dataframe` or `st.table`.

Additionally, you can check many other details for widgets like labels or disabled status. Many parameters are available for inspection, but not all. Use linting software to see what is currently supported. Here's an example:

```python
import streamlit as st

st.selectbox("A", [1,2,3], None, help="Pick a number", placeholder="Pick me")
```

```python
assert at.selectbox[0].value == None
assert at.selectbox[0].label == "A"
assert at.selectbox[0].options == ["1","2","3"]
assert at.selectbox[0].index == None
assert at.selectbox[0].help == "Pick a number"
assert at.selectbox[0].placeholder == "Pick me"
assert at.selectbox[0].disabled == False
```

<Tip>

Note that the `options` for `st.selectbox` were declared as integers but asserted as strings. As noted in the documentation for [`st.selectbox`](/develop/api-reference/widgets/st.selectbox), options are cast internally to strings. If you ever find yourself getting unexpected results, check the documentation carefully for any notes about recasting types internally.

</Tip>

retrieved_sources.title: st.selectbox could be typed so that it always returns T unless the index is None (etc)
retrieved_sources.text:
### Summary

Currently, the return type of [selectbox](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/1b73b444fe118b65f20957166f216b0e83a23e00/lib/streamlit/elements/widgets/selectbox.py#L79) is `T | None`. As far as I know, the only way for selectbox to return `None` is if `index` is `None` or if `OptionSequence[T]` is empty (`OptionSequence[]`?). These conditions could be added to the type signature of selectbox using [overloads](https://mypy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/more_types.html#function-overloading), and then in my program I wouldn't have to `assert` or `str` the results of every st.selectbox. There would be one or two overloads that returned `None | T` and one that returned just `T`. NoReturn could also possibly be added to the return type union, because if you choose an invalid index the function will error and never return.

Or maybe this goal is doomed. My project uses a lot of https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/api-reference/caching-and-state/st.session_state#session-state-and-widget-state-association stuff like:

```python
import streamlit as st
st.session_state.name = "Max"
st.selectbox("Your name", ["Sam", "Max"], key="name")
```

and I don't really know how to account for this in static typing, because the program could set the session_state value of the widget to `None`.

Furthermore, it may be unavoidable that there's always the possibility of an error in rendering, or suchlike, that would cause the widget to return None. I don't know enough to say.

So, I think this typing feature is desirable, but it may be impossible.

**Notable Changes**

- 🎛 The `on_change="ignore"` mode reaches three more widgets, so a new value updates the widget and any bound query parameter without a rerun:
    - [`st.number_input`](/develop/api-reference/widgets/st.number_input) ([#16649](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/16649)).
    - [`st.select_slider`](/develop/api-reference/widgets/st.select_slider) ([#16776](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/16776)).
    - [`st.selectbox`](/develop/api-reference/widgets/st.selectbox) ([#16862](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/16862)).
- 👻 The `mapbox.token` config option is removed. Set the `MAPBOX_API_KEY` environment variable, or pass PyDeck `api_keys` instead ([#16774](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/16774), [#16676](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/16676), [#16678](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/16678)).

**Other Changes**

retrieved_sources.title: dataframes
retrieved_sources.text:
### Validate input

When specifying a column configuration, you can declare not only the data type of the column but also value restrictions. All column configuration elements allow you to make a column required with the keyword parameter `required=True`.

For Text and Link columns, you can specify the maximum number of characters with `max_chars` or use regular expressions to validate entries through `validate`. Numerical columns, including Number, Date, Time, and Datetime have `min_value` and `max_value` parameters. Selectbox columns have a configurable list of `options`.

The data type for Number columns is `float` by default. Passing a value of type `int` to any of `min_value`, `max_value`, `step`, or `default` will set the type for the column as `int`.

retrieved_sources.title: widget-behavior
retrieved_sources.section: Widgets return simple Python data types
retrieved_sources.text:
### Widgets return simple Python data types

The value of a widget as seen through `st.session_state` and returned by the widget function are of simple Python types. For example, `st.button` returns a boolean value and will have the same boolean value saved in `st.session_state` if using a key. The first time a widget function is called (before a user interacts with it), it will return its default value. For example, `st.selectbox` returns the first option by default. Default values are configurable for all widgets with a few special exceptions like `st.button` and `st.file_uploader`.

### Summary

Passing a typed variable of int | None to the value parameter for number_input returns a float | None type.

I expected this to be int | None, and that this is how you are expected to create an empty input field, that accepts integers only, assuming the step parameter would default to 1, but it appears that strictly requires value to be int.

If you set step=1, then static type checking works as expected, resolving to int | None.

### Reproducible Code Example

```Python
import streamlit as st

default_value: int | None = None

number = st.number_input(
    "Input number",
    value=default_value,
)

if number:
    assert isinstance(number, int)
    print('Number is an int')
```

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Run example
2. Input number

### Expected Behavior

Prints 'Number is an int'

### Current Behavior

Assertion fails.

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.59.1
- Python version: 3.12
- Operating System: Windows
- Browser: Edge


### Additional Information

_No response_

```Python
import streamlit as st
st.header("Minimal example.")
selection1=st.selectbox("Select (normal)",["a","b","c"], None, key="select_normal")
st.write(selection1) #writes `None`, as expected.

if "select_keyed" not in st.session_state: st.session_state["select_keyed"] = None
if st.button("reset the keyed"):
  st.session_state["select_keyed"] = None
selection2=st.selectbox("Select (keyed)", ["a","b","c"], key="select_keyed")
st.write(selection2) #writes `None`, as expected, until you interact with any other widget, in which case it will become `a` instead.
st.text_input("You can also type something here and press enter to trigger the bug.")

st.session_state
```

retrieved_sources.title: st.selectbox could be typed so that it always returns T unless the index is None (etc)
retrieved_sources.text:
### Summary

Currently, the return type of [selectbox](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/1b73b444fe118b65f20957166f216b0e83a23e00/lib/streamlit/elements/widgets/selectbox.py#L79) is `T | None`. As far as I know, the only way for selectbox to return `None` is if `index` is `None` or if `OptionSequence[T]` is empty (`OptionSequence[]`?). These conditions could be added to the type signature of selectbox using [overloads](https://mypy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/more_types.html#function-overloading), and then in my program I wouldn't have to `assert` or `str` the results of every st.selectbox. There would be one or two overloads that returned `None | T` and one that returned just `T`. NoReturn could also possibly be added to the return type union, because if you choose an invalid index the function will error and never return.

Or maybe this goal is doomed. My project uses a lot of https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/api-reference/caching-and-state/st.session_state#session-state-and-widget-state-association stuff like:

```python
import streamlit as st
st.session_state.name = "Max"
st.selectbox("Your name", ["Sam", "Max"], key="name")
```

and I don't really know how to account for this in static typing, because the program could set the session_state value of the widget to `None`.

Furthermore, it may be unavoidable that there's always the possibility of an error in rendering, or suchlike, that would cause the widget to return None. I don't know enough to say.

So, I think this typing feature is desirable, but it may be impossible.

retrieved_sources.text:
### How to inspect elements

All elements, including widgets, have a universal `.value` property. This returns the contents of the element. For widgets, this is the same as the return value or value in Session State. For non-input elements, this will be the value of the primary contents argument. For example, `.value` returns the value of `body` for `st.markdown` or `st.error`. It returns the value of `data` for `st.dataframe` or `st.table`.

Additionally, you can check many other details for widgets like labels or disabled status. Many parameters are available for inspection, but not all. Use linting software to see what is currently supported. Here's an example:

```python
import streamlit as st

st.selectbox("A", [1,2,3], None, help="Pick a number", placeholder="Pick me")
```

```python
assert at.selectbox[0].value == None
assert at.selectbox[0].label == "A"
assert at.selectbox[0].options == ["1","2","3"]
assert at.selectbox[0].index == None
assert at.selectbox[0].help == "Pick a number"
assert at.selectbox[0].placeholder == "Pick me"
assert at.selectbox[0].disabled == False
```

<Tip>

Note that the `options` for `st.selectbox` were declared as integers but asserted as strings. As noted in the documentation for [`st.selectbox`](/develop/api-reference/widgets/st.selectbox), options are cast internally to strings. If you ever find yourself getting unexpected results, check the documentation carefully for any notes about recasting types internally.

</Tip>

retrieved_sources.section: Widgets return simple Python data types
retrieved_sources.text:
### Widgets return simple Python data types

The value of a widget as seen through `st.session_state` and returned by the widget function are of simple Python types. For example, `st.button` returns a boolean value and will have the same boolean value saved in `st.session_state` if using a key. The first time a widget function is called (before a user interacts with it), it will return its default value. For example, `st.selectbox` returns the first option by default. Default values are configurable for all widgets with a few special exceptions like `st.button` and `st.file_uploader`.

packets.initial_report:
Device Bound Session Credentials (DBSC) for st.login() sessions

### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Add opt-in support for Device Bound Session Credentials (DBSC) to the native authentication flow, so the _streamlit_user cookie set by st.login() becomes useless when copied off the device it was issued on.

Currently only Chrome takes advantage of this but I am happy to implement it and open a pull request
W3C draft: https://w3c.github.io/webappsec-dbsc/

### Why?

Since 1.42, st.login() stores the user's identity in a signed cookie with a 30-day lifetime. The cookie is HttpOnly and Secure, which is right, but there is no server-side session state: a cookie copied from a browser profile by malware or a colleague with the laptop works on any other machine until it expires, and st.logout() only clears the local copy. The app-level mitigations available today are shortening the session age in application code and re-checking an allowlist on every rerun. Neither stops a stolen cookie from being used within its window.

DBSC is the web platform's answer to exactly this. The browser generates a key pair in the device's secure hardware at login, and the server issues a short-lived cookie that the browser can only renew by signing a challenge with that key. A copied cookie expires within minutes and cannot be refreshed elsewhere. Chrome shipped it as generally available on Windows in Chrome 146 and is rolling it out on macOS in Chrome 147, and it is a W3C WebAppSec draft. Browsers without support ignore the header and keep working as today, so it degrades cleanly.

Streamlit apps are frequently internal dashboards with real data behind Google or Entra logins, which is the population this protects.

### How?

The change is contained in the Starlette auth layer and needs no frontend work. Sketch:

1. **Registration header.** In the OAuth callback, alongside the existing cookies, send `Secure-Session-Registration` pointing at a new route, with the supported algorithms (ES256, RS256).
2. **Two new routes** next to `/auth/login`, `/auth/logout` and `/auth/callback`:
   - `/auth/dbsc/register`: verifies the browser's signed registration JWT, records the device public key, returns the session config, and sets a short-lived `__Host-` bound cookie.
   - `/auth/dbsc/refresh`: on a missing or expired bound cookie the browser calls this with a signed challenge; the server verifies it against the registered key and reissues the bound cookie.
3. **Stateless key storage.** Streamlit has no server-side session store and runs as one process, so rather than adding one, the device key's thumbprint is written into the existing signed `_streamlit_user` cookie at registration. Refresh verifies the challenge signature against the thumbprint carried in the cookie. Restarts and multiple replicas are then unaffected, matching how the current cookie works.
4. **Websocket check.** The `/_stcore/stream` endpoint, which already decodes the identity cookie on connect, refuses a connection whose identity cookie is bound but whose bound cookie is absent.
5. **Configuration.** A new `[auth]` option, off by default, for example `device_bound_sessions = true`. Requires HTTPS, since `__Host-` cookies are refused otherwise, which is already true of production `st.login()` deployments.

Signature verification can use authlib's JOSE support, which is already a dependency of the auth feature.

One point to verify during implementation: Chrome defers ordinary requests while it refreshes an expired bound cookie, and the behaviour for a WebSocket upgrade is not spelled out in the spec. The frontend fetches `/_stcore/host-config` and `/_stcore/health` over HTTP before opening the stream, which should trigger the refresh first, but this needs a real-browser test.


### Additional Context

- Chrome for Developers, DBSC overview and server integration: https://developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform/device-bound-session-credentials
- Chrome 147 macOS rollout: https://scotthelme.co.uk/device-bound-session-credentials-lands-in-chrome-on-macos/

Add opt-in support for Device Bound Session Credentials (DBSC) to the native authentication flow, so the _streamlit_user cookie set by st.login() becomes useless when copied off the device it was issued on.

Since 1.42, st.login() stores the user's identity in a signed cookie with a 30-day lifetime. The cookie is HttpOnly and Secure, which is right, but there is no server-side session state: a cookie copied from a browser profile by malware or a colleague with the laptop works on any other machine until it expires, and st.logout() only clears the local copy. The app-level mitigations available today are shortening the session age in application code and re-checking an allowlist on every rerun. Neither stops a stolen cookie from being used within its window.

DBSC is the web platform's answer to exactly this. The browser generates a key pair in the device's secure hardware at login, and the server issues a short-lived cookie that the browser can only renew by signing a challenge with that key. A copied cookie expires within minutes and cannot be refreshed elsewhere. Chrome shipped it as generally available on Windows in Chrome 146 and is rolling it out on macOS in Chrome 147, and it is a W3C WebAppSec draft. Browsers without support ignore the header and keep working as today, so it degrades cleanly.

Streamlit apps are frequently internal dashboards with real data behind Google or Entra logins, which is the population this protects.

The change is contained in the Starlette auth layer and needs no frontend work. Sketch:

1. **Registration header.** In the OAuth callback, alongside the existing cookies, send `Secure-Session-Registration` pointing at a new route, with the supported algorithms (ES256, RS256).

```authlib.integrations.base_client.errors.OAuthError: invalid_request: AADSTS900144: The request body must contain the following parameter: 'client_id'. ```

```Python
import streamlit as st

if not st.user.is_logged_in:
    if st.button("Log in"):
        st.login()
    
else:
    if st.button("Log out"):
        st.logout()

    st.write(f"Hello, {st.user['name']}!")
```

    else:

page = st.navigation(pages)
page.run()

```
